hook.text: In 1989, a physicist at CERN wanted a better way to share research papers.

buildup.text: Tim Berners-Lee proposed linking documents through clickable text — hyperlinks.

discovery.text: He built the first browser, server, and website on a single NeXT computer.

twist.text: CERN almost rejected it. His boss wrote 'vague but exciting' on the cover page.

climax.text: CERN made the technology free and open. Anyone could build on it without paying.

punchline.text: The web was born from a memo marked 'vague.'

quiz.question: What did Tim Berners-Lee create the web to share?

hook.text: On December 20, 1990, the world's first website went live. It was just text and links.

buildup.text: Hosted at info.cern.ch, it explained what the World Wide Web was and how to use it.

discovery.text: No images, no colors, no design. Just blue underlined hyperlinks on a gray page.

twist.text: The original page was lost for years. CERN restored it in 2013 as a digital artifact.

climax.text: That plain text page launched an industry now worth trillions of dollars.

punchline.text: The first website was about websites.

quiz.question: What was the first website about?

topics.title: HTML: The Language of the Web

hook.text: Every website you've ever visited is built on the same simple language: HTML.

buildup.text:
HTML uses tags like

for paragraphs and for links to structure content.

discovery.text: Berners-Lee based HTML on SGML, a markup language IBM created for legal documents.

twist.text: HTML was designed to be forgiving. If a browser hit a bad tag, it just skipped it.

climax.text: That forgiveness made HTML nearly impossible to break, helping the web grow fast.

punchline.text: A forgiving language conquered the world.

quiz.question: What language was HTML based on?

hook.text: Every page on the internet has a unique address. We call it a URL.

buildup.text: URLs combine a protocol, domain name, and path into one string a browser can follow.

discovery.text: Berners-Lee designed URLs so any document could be linked from any other document.

twist.text: He later called the double slash in 'http://' a mistake he wished he could undo.

climax.text: Despite that regret, URLs became the address system for all human knowledge online.

punchline.text: Every idea on the web starts with an address.

quiz.question: What did Berners-Lee regret about URLs?

topics.title: HTTP: How Browsers Talk to Servers

hook.text: When you click a link, your browser sends a message to a server asking for a page.

buildup.text: That message follows HTTP, a protocol Tim Berners-Lee wrote in 1991.

discovery.text: HTTP is like a polite chat: the browser requests, and the server responds.

twist.text: Early HTTP opened a new connection for every file. Images meant dozens of handshakes.

climax.text: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 fixed this, letting pages load in a fraction of a second.

punchline.text: The web runs on a 1991 conversation style.

quiz.question: What problem did early HTTP have?
options: A new connection for every file

hook.text: Before 1993, the web was text-only. Then a student in Illinois changed everything.

buildup.text: Marc Andreessen built Mosaic, the first browser to show images inline with text.

discovery.text: Suddenly the web was visual. People could see photos, logos, and graphics on a page.

twist.text: Academics mocked it as dumbing down the internet. They preferred text-only Gopher.

climax.text: Within a year, web traffic grew 341,000%. Mosaic made the web a mass medium.

punchline.text: One browser turned the web from text to visual.

quiz.question: What did Mosaic introduce to web browsing?

hook.text: In 1994, anyone could build a homepage for free. GeoCities gave everyone a web address.

buildup.text: Users picked a 'neighborhood' — Hollywood for fun, SiliconValley for tech.

discovery.text: Millions created pages with animated GIFs, visitor counters, and blinking text.

twist.text: Yahoo bought GeoCities for $3.6 billion, then shut it down ten years later.

climax.text: Archivists raced to save millions of personal pages before they vanished forever.

punchline.text: The first social web died with a corporate memo.

quiz.question: Who bought and later shut down GeoCities?

hook.text: Early web designers had no layout tools. So they hijacked HTML tables meant for data.

buildup.text: By nesting invisible tables, designers forced pixels into the positions they wanted.

discovery.text: Table layouts let designers create magazine-style pages for the first time.

twist.text: The code was a nightmare — a simple page could have tables nested ten levels deep.

climax.text: Screen readers couldn't parse the mess. Accessibility was an afterthought.

punchline.text: The web's first layouts were beautiful hacks.

quiz.question: Why did early designers use HTML tables for layout?

topics.title: The GIF and Early Web Graphics

hook.text: The GIF format was invented in 1987 — six years before it conquered the web.

buildup.text: GIF supported animation and transparency, perfect for the colorful early web.

discovery.text: Dancing babies, spinning skulls, 'Under Construction' signs — GIFs defined 90s web culture.

twist.text: A patent dispute over GIF's compression nearly killed the format in the late 90s.

climax.text: The patent expired in 2004. GIFs came roaring back as the internet's reaction format.

punchline.text: A 1987 format still dominates web culture.

quiz.question: What nearly killed the GIF format in the late 1990s?

topics.title: View Source: Learning in the Open

hook.text: Early web developers had no tutorials. They learned by reading other people's code.

buildup.text: Every browser had a 'View Source' button that revealed the HTML behind any page.

discovery.text: An entire generation taught themselves web development by copying and tweaking source code.

twist.text: No other medium worked this way. You couldn't 'view source' on a TV show or magazine.

climax.text: That radical transparency created the web's culture of sharing and open knowledge.

punchline.text: The web taught people how to build it.

quiz.question: How did early developers learn web development?
options: Using View Source on other sites

hook.text: Static HTML pages couldn't respond to users. Every visitor saw the exact same thing.

buildup.text: CGI let servers run a program when a user submitted a form or clicked a link.

discovery.text: Web pages could finally show search results, guest books, and hit counters.

twist.text: Every request launched a new process on the server. Ten visitors meant ten programs.

climax.text: CGI was slow and fragile, but it proved the web could be more than a brochure.

punchline.text: Interactivity started with one clunky script.

quiz.question: What was a key problem with CGI scripts?
options: Each request launched a new process
They only worked in Internet Explorer

hook.text: In 1995, Rasmus Lerdorf created a tool to track visits to his online resume.

buildup.text: That tool evolved into PHP — a language you could embed directly inside HTML.

discovery.text: PHP made dynamic pages easy. Mix code with markup and the server handled the rest.

twist.text: Purists hated PHP's messy design. But it powered WordPress, Facebook, and Wikipedia.

climax.text: By 2010, PHP ran nearly 80% of all websites with server-side code.

punchline.text: A resume tracker became the web's engine.

quiz.question: What did PHP originally start as?

hook.text: Netscape needed a scripting language for the browser. They gave one engineer ten days.

buildup.text: Brendan Eich created JavaScript in May 1995, originally calling it Mocha.

discovery.text: It let web pages respond to clicks, validate forms, and change content without reloading.

twist.text: The name 'JavaScript' was a marketing trick to ride Java's hype. They're unrelated.

climax.text: That rushed prototype became the most widely used programming language on Earth.

punchline.text: Ten days created the web's default language.

quiz.question: How long did it take Brendan Eich to create JavaScript?

hook.text: In the late 90s, the web couldn't play video, animate smoothly, or run games.

buildup.text: Macromedia Flash filled every gap with animation, sound, and rich interactivity.

discovery.text: Entire websites were built in Flash — immersive experiences impossible with HTML.

twist.text: Flash didn't work on iPhones. Steve Jobs wrote an open letter refusing to support it.

climax.text: Adobe killed Flash in 2020. The open web standards it inspired had already replaced it.

punchline.text: Flash showed what the web could be, then died.

quiz.question: Why was Flash ultimately abandoned?

hook.text: Early websites styled everything inline. Change a font and you'd edit hundreds of pages.

buildup.text: CSS proposed separating a page's appearance from its structure completely.

discovery.text: One stylesheet could control an entire website's look with a single file change.

twist.text: Browsers implemented CSS inconsistently. The same code looked different everywhere.

climax.text: Designers fought browser quirks for years. Eventually standards won and CSS unified.

punchline.text: Style and structure were never meant to mix.

quiz.question: What was the main benefit CSS introduced?

hook.text: Before 2005, clicking anything on a web page meant waiting for a full page reload.

buildup.text: AJAX let browsers fetch data quietly and update just part of a page.

discovery.text: Google Maps proved the power — users dragged maps smoothly without any reloads.

twist.text: AJAX wasn't new. Microsoft invented the core XMLHttpRequest object back in 1999.

climax.text: It took six years and a killer demo for developers to realize what they already had.

punchline.text: The web got faster by asking for less.

quiz.question: Which app famously demonstrated AJAX's potential?

hook.text: In the early 2000s, publishing online required technical skill. Blogs changed that.

buildup.text: Platforms like Blogger and WordPress let anyone publish with a few clicks.

discovery.text: Millions found a voice. Personal journals, political takes, and news poured online.

twist.text: Blogs challenged traditional media. Some bloggers broke stories before newspapers.

climax.text: The blog revolution proved the web's real power was giving everyone a printing press.

punchline.text: Everyone became a publisher overnight.

quiz.question: What did blogging platforms democratize?

hook.text: MySpace launched in 2003 and let users customize profiles with HTML and CSS.

buildup.text: Facebook followed with a cleaner design and a focus on real identity.

discovery.text: Social networks turned the web from a collection of pages into a stream of updates.

twist.text: People stopped visiting websites. The web came to them through feeds and notifications.

climax.text: By 2010, social media consumed more attention than email, search, and news combined.

punchline.text: The web shifted from pages to people.

quiz.question: What did MySpace let users do with their profiles?

hook.text: Wikipedia launched in 2001 with zero articles. Volunteers wrote everything.

buildup.text: YouTube followed in 2005, letting anyone upload video without technical knowledge.

discovery.text: The web's content was no longer made by professionals. Users became the creators.

twist.text: Platforms profited enormously from free labor. Creators rarely saw the revenue.

climax.text: User-generated content became the foundation of the entire internet economy.

punchline.text: Users built the web companies monetized.

quiz.question: What did Wikipedia launch with in 2001?

hook.text: In the early web, every site was an island. Data stayed locked inside each platform.

buildup.text: Web APIs opened doors, letting services expose their data through simple endpoints.

discovery.text: Developers combined maps, weather, and social data into new apps called mashups.

twist.text: Companies realized APIs were products. Twitter, Google, and Stripe built empires on them.

climax.text: Today the average web page makes dozens of API calls you never see.

punchline.text: APIs turned the web into a connected machine.

quiz.question: What are 'mashups' in web development?

hook.text: In 2007, Steve Jobs showed a full web browser that fit in your pocket.

buildup.text: Sites designed for big monitors had to squeeze onto a tiny 320-pixel screen.

discovery.text: Pinching and zooming desktop sites was painful. The web needed a fresh approach.

twist.text: Apple refused to support Flash, forcing developers to rebuild with open standards.

climax.text: The iPhone didn't just add a screen size. It forced the entire web to rethink design.

punchline.text: A phone broke the desktop web's monopoly.

quiz.question: What did Apple refuse to support on the iPhone?

hook.text: By 2010, phones, tablets, and desktops all needed different website layouts.

buildup.text: Ethan Marcotte proposed responsive design: one site that adapts to any screen.

discovery.text: Fluid grids, flexible images, and media queries let layouts reshape themselves.

twist.text: Before this idea, companies maintained entirely separate mobile and desktop sites.

climax.text: Responsive design killed the 'm-dot' era and became the standard for all new sites.

punchline.text: One design to fit every screen.

quiz.question: Who coined the term 'responsive web design'?

hook.text: Responsive design started with desktop and squeezed down. Mobile-first flipped that.

buildup.text: Luke Wroblewski argued: design for the smallest screen first, then scale up.

discovery.text: Starting small forced designers to prioritize content and cut unnecessary clutter.

twist.text: By 2016, mobile traffic surpassed desktop globally. Mobile-first became common sense.

climax.text: Google ranked sites by their mobile version, rewarding mobile-first design.

punchline.text: Small screens taught designers what mattered.

quiz.question: When did mobile traffic surpass desktop globally?

topics.title: App Stores vs. the Open Web

hook.text: Apple's App Store launched in 2008 with 500 apps. Within a year it had 65,000.

buildup.text: Native apps were faster and smoother than mobile websites. Developers followed the money.

discovery.text: Users spent 90% of mobile time in apps, not browsers. The open web seemed to lose.

twist.text: But apps needed downloads, updates, and store approval. The web had none of that.

climax.text: The tension between closed apps and the open web shaped a decade of technology.

punchline.text: Apps won attention; the web kept its freedom.

quiz.question: How many apps did the App Store launch with in 2008?

hook.text: What if a website could work offline, send push alerts, and feel like a native app?

buildup.text: Google proposed Progressive Web Apps in 2015 — websites with app-like powers.

discovery.text: Service workers let sites cache content and function without an internet connection.

twist.text: Apple dragged its feet on PWA support, protecting App Store revenue.

climax.text: PWAs proved the web could close the gap with native apps, no download required.

punchline.text: Websites learned to work offline.

quiz.question: What technology lets PWAs work offline?

hook.text: Traditional websites load a new page for every click. SPAs changed that completely.

buildup.text: Single-page apps load once, then swap content without full page refreshes.

discovery.text: Gmail and Google Maps pioneered the approach, feeling more like desktop software.

twist.text: SPAs broke the back button, confused search engines, and overcomplicated simple sites.

climax.text: The industry spent a decade optimizing SPAs, then asked if simpler was better.

punchline.text: Speed came at the cost of simplicity.

quiz.question: What is a key characteristic of single-page applications?

hook.text: By 2015, many developers were tired of slow, complex server-side architectures.

buildup.text: JAMstack proposed a simpler model: pre-build pages and serve them from a CDN.

discovery.text: Static sites with JavaScript and APIs could be fast, secure, and cheap to host.

twist.text: Critics said JAMstack just renamed what people were already doing. The brand stuck.

climax.text: Netlify and Vercel built billion-dollar companies around this simpler approach.

punchline.text: The simplest architecture won the argument.

quiz.question: What does JAMstack serve pages from?

hook.text: Every framework invented its own way to create reusable UI pieces.

buildup.text: Web Components offered a browser-native solution with custom elements and Shadow DOM.

discovery.text: Developers could create encapsulated, reusable widgets without any framework.

twist.text: React and Vue moved faster. Web Components arrived too late to stop the framework wars.

climax.text: But standards outlast hype. Web Components are now supported in every major browser.

punchline.text: Standards move slow but last forever.

quiz.question: What browser feature do Web Components use for encapsulation?

hook.text: Running web servers meant renting hardware and managing operating systems around the clock.

buildup.text: Serverless let developers deploy functions without thinking about servers at all.

discovery.text: AWS Lambda launched in 2014. Write a function, upload it, and Amazon ran it for you.

twist.text: The name was misleading. Servers still existed — you just couldn't see them.

climax.text: Serverless let a solo developer scale like a Fortune 500 company.

punchline.text: The servers didn't vanish; they just hid.

quiz.question: When did AWS Lambda launch?

hook.text: The web started as linked documents. Now it runs 3D games, video editors, and AI.

buildup.text: WebAssembly, WebGPU, and modern APIs turned browsers into full application platforms.

discovery.text: Figma runs in the browser. Photoshop has a web version. VS Code works online.

twist.text: Desktop apps are migrating to the web, not the other way around.

climax.text: The browser became the operating system nobody predicted back in 1989.

punchline.text: The browser is the new operating system.

quiz.question: What technology lets compiled code run in the browser at near-native speed?
